Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-13
Start time (UTC): 16:00
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Sofia (Redwood AE), Diego (SE), Jun (Runtime Eng) - Maya (Cerulean CTO), Ethan (Lead ML Infra), Priya (SRE)

[00:00:00] Sofia: hey everyone, thanks for joining. we'll kick off the deep dive. Diego and Jun from our runtime team are here to go into profiling details. maya, ethan, priya, thanks for making time.
[00:00:30] Maya: yeah thanks, uh we are excited; we've been seeing jitter on tail latency when we scale to bursts and want to understand whether tensorRT-llm or vllm path is better for our 8k-context models.
[00:01:05] Diego: cool. quick agenda: kernel selection, cudagraphs, kv cache interplay, batching strategies, quant, then Q&A + next steps. sound good?
[00:01:25] Ethan: yep that works. our targets: p95 < 180ms at 8 tokens, sustained 250 qps across a 4-node H100 pool.
[00:01:55] Jun: ok good, that's a useful target. first, kernel selection: we saw with your model shapes (wide dense layers, long attention spans) that kernel choice matters a lot -- some fusion kernels (fused attention+mlp) on TRT-LLM outperform generic aten kernels in vLLM, but cost is model-shape specific.
[00:02:30] Maya: when you say "cost" do you mean total token cost or inference latency cost?
[00:02:40] Jun: latency mostly. fused kernels reduce per-token latency significantly for medium sequence lengths, but they require model conversion and sometimes custom tuning.
[00:03:10] Diego: right, and vLLM path can be faster for very short sequences because it avoids the extra conversion step and keeps execution path simpler; but vLLM's kernels can lose on larger batch sizes or longer contexts where TensorRT's optimized matmul kernels shine.
[00:03:45] Priya: hmm we've been seeing high memory variance. is that kv cache behavior?
[00:03:55] Jun: partially. kv cache allocation and sharding matters. TRT-LLM tends to manage kv cache more tightly when the model is converted to the TRT engine, whereas in vLLM we rely on framework-managed KV which can be more fragmented especially with dynamic batching.
[00:04:30] [00:04:30] Diego: we have some slides and traces -- i'm going to share a cudagraph trace from a recent run (link: /redwood-shared/cudagraphs/cerulean-sample1).
[00:04:45] Maya: saw the link, thanks.
[00:04:55] Diego: so this trace is an 8k context run, batch size 1 to emulate low-latency single-user flows; you can see that when we warm up a cudagraph for the prefix+decode steps, per-token latency becomes very consistent -- p95 drops by ~30-40ms after warmup in our tests.
[00:05:25] Ethan: that warmup overhead is a concern for ephemeral containers; we run a lot of short-lived containers in our on-prem k8s.
[00:05:40] Jun: totally. cudagraphs are best in long-lived workers or Dedicated pools (where you can amortize warmup). for transient serverless we prefer continuous-batching + prefix cache to avoid graph rebuilds.
[00:06:05] Priya: can you explain the prefix cache tradeoff again?
[00:06:12] Diego: yeah. prefix or KV caching stores the attention keys/values for repeated prefixes -- for chat-style multi-turn traffic, this can avoid recomputing the encoder/prefix. it reduces compute and latency but increases memory pressure; you need eviction policies.
[00:06:40] Maya: and does TRT-LLM handle eviction differently?
[00:06:45] Jun: TRT-LLM converted engines can pin kv layouts which lets us optimize GPU memory layout, so eviction becomes deterministic and cheaper. vLLM's dynamic allocations give flexibility but fragmentation can cause tail spikes.
[00:07:20] [00:07:20] Diego: moving on to batching: we ran two modes -- aggressive batching for throughput and conservative batching with latency SLOs. for your target p95 180ms, our recommendation is small max batch sizes (2-4) with a 20-30ms batching window, plus preferential routing for low-latency tokens.
[00:07:50] Ethan: curious, what's the throughput difference? numbers?
[00:07:56] Diego: in our lab: on H100, for your model family, TRT-LLM with cudagraphs and fused kernels achieved ~1.8x higher tokens/sec at 64 token sequences vs vLLM baseline with aten kernels. but for 8-token bursts, vLLM had slightly lower median latency by ~10-15ms pre-warmup.
[00:08:35] Priya: what's the memory overhead of TRT engines vs vLLM?
[00:08:40] Jun: TRT engines increase binary size and can require extra workspace memory; quantized TRT engines reduce memory but require calibration. vLLM's memory usage is more predictable but can include fragmentation.
[00:09:05] Maya: ok. quantization -- we ran int8 in dev and saw ~8% accuracy drop on one benchmark. any ways to mitigate?
[00:09:20] Jun: calibration and per-channel quant can help; also mixed-precision (FP16+int8 for activations) reduces regressions. we recommend running eval suites tied to your key prompts; Redwood Optimize can help automate that.
[00:09:50] Diego: also note that TensorRT offers QDQ patterns and per-layer tuning that can get you closer to FP16 accuracy. but it's work: you'd need representative calibration data.
[00:10:20] [00:10:20] Maya: does the KV cache lose correctness with quantization?
[00:10:30] Jun: no inherent correctness loss if implemented carefully, but quant noise can accumulate in long contexts; we saw small drift in 8k scenarios if everything is int8. Mixed precision is safer for long chats.
[00:10:55] Ethan: about cudagraphs -- any gotchas with dynamic sequence lengths? our user traffic varies a lot.
[00:11:05] Diego: cudagraphs assume a static graph shape; for variable lengths you either build a family of graphs (for common seq bins) or fall back to non-graph path for tails. building many graphs increases memory and management complexity.
[00:11:40] Priya: so for our mixed traffic maybe a hybrid: graphs for hot paths and vLLM for rare long tails?
[00:11:50] Jun: exactly. and Redwood routing can direct traffic by route: hot route -> Dedicated TRT engines with graphs, rare -> hosted vLLM fallback.
[00:12:15] Maya: does that complicate consistency of results? model variants might differ.
[00:12:25] Diego: model outputs can vary slightly due to kernel differences and quant; we recommend A/B tests and model-aligned rollouts. Redwood has eval hooks to compare outputs.
[00:12:55] [00:12:55] Ethan: security question -- for on-prem/H100 racks, we need KMS and isolated VPC. how does the runtime behave with private deployments?
[00:13:05] Jun: Private deployments run the same runtime; we package TRT-compiled engines and runtime as a container. KMS/HSM integration for keys is supported, and audit logs are emitted. the main ops work is provisioning a Dedicated pool so graphs can persist.
[00:13:40] Maya: any special kernel licensing or third-party constraints for TRT-LLM?
[00:13:48] Diego: TensorRT has its own licensing but it's fine for enterprise deployments; there's no extra runtime licensing from Redwood. some third-party fused kernels may have limited availability, we'll note any constraints.
[00:14:20] [00:14:20] Priya: can we see a concrete profiling output? like nvtx/nvprof spans?
[00:14:28] Diego: yes we have an excerpt -- i'm pasting a snippet in chat (link: /redwood-shared/profiles/cerulean-nvtx-20261210.txt). you can see large peaks at attention and matmul before we apply fused kernels. after fusion, the matmul spans shrink and memory copies reduce.
[00:15:00] Jun: one important metric is kernel occupancy vs achieved gflops -- we sometimes prefer a slightly lower occupancy kernel with higher arithmetic intensity. the profiler numbers will show that.
[00:15:30] Maya: what about multi-instance GPU (MIG) or CUDA MPS? we currently use MPS on clouds.
[00:15:40] Jun: MPS helps with small-batch latency by multiplexing SMs, but it increases jitter in noisy neighbors. MIG isolates performance but can reduce peak perf for large kernels. we recommend Dedicated H100 slices for stable high throughput; for latency-sensitive small workloads MPS can help but test carefully.
[00:16:15] [00:16:15] Diego: we briefly tested MIG with TRT engines and saw deterministic behavior for some models but not all -- again model-shape dependent.
[00:16:35] Ethan: can Redwood's optimizer suggest kernel choices automatically? we have limited in-house runtime expertise.
[00:16:45] Diego: yes, Redwood Optimize can run microbenchmarks across kernel candidates and propose a kernel selection matrix per model/profile. Jun can show a sample matrix after the call.
[00:17:10] Jun: here's a sample rule: if seq_len < 32 and batch <=4, prefer aten-fused path in vLLM; if seq_len >= 128 or batch >=16, prefer TRT fused matmul kernels with cudagraphs. of course these are heuristics.
[00:17:40] [00:17:40] Priya: about continuous batching -- how do you maintain latency SLOs for interactive routes?
[00:17:50] Diego: we use priority queues and token-budget windows. low-latency routes have small windows and higher scheduling priority; background routes are pooled for throughput. you can configure per-route SLOs.
[00:18:20] Maya: any specific advice for our deployment shape? we will likely run an on-prem Dedicated pool behind an SSO-protected API gateway.
[00:18:30] Jun: for on-prem: pin a set of H100 GPUs with persistent worker processes, pre-build cudagraphs for common seq bins, enable prefix caching for known session patterns, and use mixed-precision quant for memory/latency wins. also ensure eviction policy for KV cache matches your user session lifetime.
[00:19:05] [00:19:05] Ethan: what about the work to convert our models to TRT-LLM? time estimate?
[00:19:12] Diego: for a typical 7B-13B LLM it's 1-2 engineer-weeks to do conversion + validation + quant calibration; for 70B+ it's longer and we recommend staged rollouts.
[00:19:40] Jun: also some ops may need plugin kernels; if we hit unsupported ops we either fallback to vLLM for those layers or implement plugin kernels.
[00:20:05] Maya: is there an example repo for conversions?
[00:20:10] Diego: yes; we'll share a conversion checklist and scripts (link: /redwood-shared/tensorrt-convert-checklist.md).
[00:20:30] [00:20:30] Priya: latency SLO monitoring -- do you expose token-level traces to customer console?
[00:20:38] Jun: yes we expose per-request token latency breakdowns, NVTX spans (aggregated), and kernel-level heatmaps in Redwood Console. you can tie regressions to specific kernel changes.
[00:21:05] Ethan: for our acceptance test -- can you run a bench with our models and produce p50/p95/p99 and memory profile across 1-16 concurrent sessions?
[00:21:15] Sofia: yes that's part of the pilot scope; we'll run lab benches and then on-prem if that looks good.
[00:21:45] [00:21:45] Diego: quick note on cudagraph rebuilds: when sequence length distribution changes dramatically, graph rebuilds can occur which spikes latency. we mitigate with graph pooling and fallback paths.
[00:22:10] Maya: any raw numbers we can expect after optimization? you mentioned 1.8x tokens/sec for certain shapes. what does that translate to for our p95 target?
[00:22:20] Diego: tentative: with TRT-LLM and cudagraphs on Dedicated, we believe you can hit p95 ~140-170ms for 8-token tails at your target QPS, assuming KV prefix hits >60%. without prefixes you'll see higher.
[00:22:50] Priya: how do we measure KV prefix hit rates?
[00:22:55] Jun: Redwood Console logs prefix hits per route; we can instrument session-level tags.
[00:23:20] [00:23:20] Maya: on monitoring and security, our compliance team requires audit logs and key access logs -- is that included in Private?
[00:23:30] Sofia: yes Private includes audit logs and KMS integration. we can provide SOC2 artifacts.
[00:23:50] Ethan: about model variant drift between TRT and vLLM -- will we need to retrain or just calibrate?
[00:23:58] Diego: mostly calibration and sometimes small prompt-engineering adjustments; retraining rarely needed unless quantization reveals model sensitivity.
[00:24:25] [00:24:25] Maya: can you summarize a recommended path step-by-step for us?
[00:24:30] Jun: sure: 1) run Redwood microbench with your models (we'll run in lab), 2) convert hot models to TRT-LLM and build cudagraphs for hot seq bins, 3) enable prefix caching for multi-turn chat, 4) enable mixed-precision quant and calibrate, 5) pilot on Dedicated on-prem pool, 6) expand with routing rules and observability.
[00:25:05] Diego: we'll provide the scripts and a recommended kernel selection matrix.
[00:25:25] [00:25:25] Maya: ok great. can we walk through a couple live traces you mentioned?
[00:25:30] Diego: yes i'll paste two nvtx timelines: pre-fusion and post-fusion. pre-fusion shows attention spans at 12ms each token, post goes down to 6-7ms for same stage. see the charts.
[00:25:55] Ethan: the charts show memory copies as biggest tail contributor; can cudagraphs eliminate those copies?
[00:26:05] Jun: they reduce them because cudagraphs can fuse memcpy patterns into the graph; but not all copies are removable -- some are model-structure dependent.
[00:26:35] [00:26:35] Priya: any tips for running bench on our k8s infra? we use ephemeral pods behind an nginx gateway.
[00:26:45] Diego: for reproducible benches use pinned nodes, disable autoscaler during bench, and run with persistent workers to allow graph warmup. we'll provide a bench playbook.
[00:27:10] Maya: what about fallback if an engine fails on a node? do you automatically route to vLLM?
[00:27:18] Sofia: yes we support automatic fallback to a compatible model variant (vLLM-hosted) with configurable grace periods so you don't see errors.
[00:27:40] [00:27:40] Ethan: are there any known ops that block TRT conversion?
[00:27:46] Jun: a handful of custom torch ops require plugin kernels; if we encounter them we either implement plugin or isolate those layers to run in aten while the rest is TRT.
[00:28:05] Diego: note this hybrid execution has a small overhead but it's manageable.
[00:28:30] [00:28:30] Maya: let's talk about testing strategy for correctness after conversion.
[00:28:36] Jun: run an eval suite of core prompts, measure token-level divergence, run end-to-end smoke tests, and a rollout with canary traffic at low percentage. Redwood's compare tool can compute divergence scores and flag regressions.
[00:29:05] Ethan: ok nice. can you run a quick demo of the comparator?
[00:29:12] Diego: we can demo in a follow-up -- it's interactive and we usually do it with customer prompts.
[00:29:35] [00:29:35] Priya: what's the typical pilot length?
[00:29:40] Sofia: pilot is usually 4-8 weeks: lab runs, conversion, on-prem bench, then a short production pilot.
[00:30:05] Maya: budget question -- cost delta between hosted vLLM and Dedicated TRT?
[00:30:12] Sofia: Dedicated has higher fixed cost but lower unit token cost at scale; we'll send estimates. for your QPS target Dedicated pilot is often cost-neutral after a few months.
[00:30:40] [00:30:40] Ethan: any more technical notes on quantization drift in long contexts?
[00:30:46] Jun: sometimes you see attention score saturation with int8; mitigation: use block-wise quant or keep attention in FP16.
[00:31:10] Diego: also monitoring for token probability shifts helps detect drift early.
[00:31:35] [00:31:35] Maya: curious about toolchain: do you support on-prem TRT compile or do we hand off artifacts?
[00:31:42] Diego: both: we can deliver compiled engines or provide the toolchain and scripts to compile in your environment. compiling on-prem is preferable for air-gapped setups.
[00:32:10] Priya: is there a recommended H100 configuration? multi-instance vs full GPU?
[00:32:18] Jun: for your workload, full-GPU Dedicated processes are best for high-throughput; use MIG only if you have many tiny concurrent hosts.
[00:32:45] [00:32:45] Diego: quick demo note -- we'll attach the kernel selection spreadsheet after call. it maps seq_len, batch, model-size to recommended engine.
[00:33:05] Maya: great. i'll want to see p99 numbers too; those matter to SLA.
[00:33:12] Diego: we'll include p99, p95, memory headroom in the bench report.
[00:33:35] [00:33:35] Ethan: any known incompatibilities with our observability stack (we run Prometheus + Grafana)?
[00:33:42] Jun: Redwood exports Prom metrics and traces; we can provide exporters and dashboards for Grafana.
[00:34:05] Priya: for the pilot, what logs will we get? nvtx spans, kernel-level timings?
[00:34:12] Diego: yes aggregated nvtx spans, kernel latency histograms, per-request token traces, and memory allocation timelines.
[00:34:40] [00:34:40] Maya: what's the recommended eviction policy for KV cache? LRU? TTL-based?
[00:34:50] Jun: LRU with a TTL for session maximum lifetime works well; for sensitive memory usage use size-based eviction combined with LRU.
[00:35:15] Diego: also consider checkpointing long sessions off-GPU if you need to free memory.
[00:35:35] [00:35:35] Maya: ok this is super helpful. any surprises you'd flag for us?
[00:35:42] Jun: main surprises: cudagraph rebuilds causing spikes, quant drift in very long contexts, and vendor-specific kernel performance differences -- all manageable but need testing.
[00:36:10] Diego: also watch memory fragmentation in vLLM under dynamic batching; it can cause p99 spikes.
[00:36:35] [00:36:35] Sofia: quick recap -- we'll run an initial lab bench, share scripts and kernel matrix, convert a hot model to TRT-LLM, and schedule on-prem pilot. next steps captured as action items.

[00:37:02] Jun: engine upgrades are atomic at worker restart; we recommend canary rolling restarts with traffic mirroring for validation.
